transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Dubois, thank you for coming in to speak with me and Nurse Sarah. I have something important to discuss with you regarding your grandson’s care this morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes. Is he alright? He seemed very sleepy when I checked on him.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: He is stable now, but I have to tell you that we made a serious mistake with his medication. I calculated his dose based on an estimate of his weight rather than weighing him on the scale. Because of that, he received a dose that was significantly higher than what is safe for a child of his size.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What? You guessed his weight?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I did. I estimated it instead of measuring it, and that was wrong. I am deeply sorry. I take full responsibility for this error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My grandson is a small boy. He is not a number on a chart. You are a doctor, yet you just... you guessed? C'est inadmissible.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is completely unacceptable. There is no excuse for not following the proper safety protocol. I know this is shocking and upsetting to hear.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Upsetting? I feel betrayed. We trust you with him. I feel as though he is just a task to be finished quickly for you.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like you feel your grandson was treated carelessly, and that his dignity and safety were overlooked. I can see why you feel that way, and I am truly sorry for the breach of trust.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: He is only four years old. He cannot tell me if he feels sick. He cannot tell me if you have poisoned him.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand your fear for him and that feeling of helplessness because he can't speak for himself. I am here to be completely transparent with you about what happens next.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what happens? Does he have brain damage? Does he have something in his blood?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The medication he received is one that we can monitor closely. Right now, his vital signs are normal. However, because the dose was too high, he is very drowsy. We need to monitor his breathing and heart rate every hour for the next twelve hours to ensure there are no delayed reactions.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want to know why this happened. If you were too busy, you should have said so.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It wasn't a matter of being too busy. It was a failure in my judgement. I should have used the scale, and I didn't. I failed him and I failed you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I do not know if I can look at you the same way.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. I have caused a great deal of distress and worry. I am the one who made this mistake, and I accept that it will take time to earn back any trust.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What are you doing now? Just watching him sleep?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, we have a specific plan. First, I have contacted the pediatric toxicology team, and they are coming to assess him within the next thirty minutes. Second, we have moved him to a room with continuous cardiac monitoring. You will be with him, and I want you to tell us immediately if you notice any change in his breathing or if he becomes difficult to wake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And for the other children? Who else are you guessing for?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am ensuring that every single weight in this ward is verified against the scale today. I have already reported this to my supervisor and the safety board so that we can change the checklist to make it impossible to enter a dose without a timestamped weight from the scale.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You speak of checklists. I speak of my grandson.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are absolutely right. The checklists are for the system, but right now, the only thing that matters is that your grandson is safe and that you are supported.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I will stay with him. I will not leave his side.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is the best place for you to be. I will be back in ten minutes to give you an update on the toxicology team's arrival. Do you have any questions about the monitoring plan for me right now?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. Just get the other doctor here.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will make sure the senior consultant comes in to see you both immediately after I speak with the toxicology team. I am very sorry, Mr. Dubois.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to express anger and betrayal without interrupting and remains regulated throughout the pushback.

E.justification: The error is named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, but there is only one comprehension check at the end.

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language, takes full personal responsibility, and maintains accountability even when the patient expresses betrayal.

R.justification: Resident specifically names emotions ('shocking and upsetting', 'fear', 'helplessness') and references the patient's specific concerns about the child's dignity.

T.justification: Resident provides specific steps (toxicology team, cardiac monitor), timelines (30 minutes, 12 hours), a patient role (reporting changes in breathing), and a prevention plan (checklist change).
